bibimbap.name: Bibimbap
bibimbap.why: Rice, seasoned vegetables and gochujang mixed in one bowl; a balanced plate for midday or evening.

kimchiJjigae.name: Kimchi jjigae
kimchiJjigae.why: A stew built on well-fermented kimchi; its sour, hot broth suits cool evenings and late nights.

tteokbokki.name: Tteokbokki
tteokbokki.why: Chewy rice cakes simmered in a gochujang sauce; Korea's default afternoon snack and late-night bite.

ramen.name: Ramen
ramen.why: Wheat noodles in a pork-bone or shoyu broth; a filling bowl at lunch and the classic post-midnight meal.

sushi.name: Sushi
sushi.why: Vinegared rice topped with raw fish; light and clean enough for lunch, composed enough for dinner.

onigiri.name: Onigiri
onigiri.why: A hand-sized rice ball wrapped in nori; eaten on the move at breakfast or as an afternoon bridge.

dimSum.name: Dim sum
dimSum.why: Steamed dumplings and small plates served with tea, the Cantonese morning-to-noon ritual of yum cha.

mapoTofu.name: Mapo tofu
mapoTofu.why: Silken tofu in a doubanjiang sauce with numbing Sichuan pepper; a rice-friendly lunch or dinner.

pho.name: Pho
pho.why: Rice noodles in a clear beef broth with fresh herbs; Vietnam's breakfast that carries into lunch.

banhMi.name: Bánh mì
banhMi.why: A crisp baguette filled with pickled vegetables, herbs and meat; quick to eat at breakfast or lunch.

padThai.name: Pad thai
padThai.why: Stir-fried rice noodles balanced with tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar; a lunch or dinner staple.

tomYum.name: Tom yum
tomYum.why: A hot and sour soup of lemongrass, chili and lime; it wakes the palate in the evening and at night.

nasiGoreng.name: Nasi goreng
nasiGoreng.why: Rice fried with kecap manis and topped with a fried egg; Indonesia's breakfast and lunch in one plate.

tacosAlPastor.name: Tacos al pastor
tacosAlPastor.why: Spit-roasted pork with pineapple on corn tortillas; Mexico City's evening and late-night street order.

neapolitanPizza.name: Neapolitan pizza
neapolitanPizza.why: A thin dough blistered in a wood-fired oven in about 90 seconds; dinner and late-night fare.

cacioEPepe.name: Cacio e pepe
cacioEPepe.why: Roman pasta finished with pecorino, black pepper and starchy water; a simple, rich dinner.

croissant.name: Croissant
croissant.why: Laminated butter dough baked into flaky layers; at its best alongside morning coffee.

shakshuka.name: Shakshuka
shakshuka.why: Eggs poached in a tomato and pepper sauce, eaten with bread; a Maghreb breakfast that stretches to lunch.

avocadoToast.name: Avocado toast
avocadoToast.why: Smashed avocado on sourdough, the Australian café breakfast that spread worldwide.

flatWhite.name: Flat white
flatWhite.why: Espresso under a thin layer of velvety milk; a morning or mid-afternoon focus cup.

pourOverCoffee.name: Pour-over coffee
pourOverCoffee.why: Filter coffee brewed slowly by hand; a clean, bright cup for the afternoon slump.

darkChocolate.name: Dark chocolate
darkChocolate.why: Seventy percent cacao or more; a small, bitter square that fits an afternoon pause.

greekSalad.name: Greek salad
greekSalad.why: Tomato, cucumber, feta and olive oil; a cool, fresh plate for warm lunches and evenings.

birria.name: Birria
birria.why: Meat braised slowly in a chili adobo, served with its rich broth; a lunch or after-dark meal.

fermentation.title: Fermentation revival
fermentation.line: Since Noma's fermentation lab and its 2018 guide, kimchi, miso and kombucha have become a shared vocabulary of restaurant kitchens.

plantForward.title: Plant-forward plates
plantForward.line: Vegetables move to the centre of the plate without going fully vegetarian; plant-based patties reached major fast-food menus in 2019.

hyperLocal.title: Hyper-local sourcing
hyperLocal.line: Kitchens source within a few dozen kilometres and print the farm or boat on the menu; the seasonal card changes with the harvest.

zeroWaste.title: Zero-waste kitchens
zeroWaste.line: Peels, bones and stems are turned into stocks, ferments and powders; the FAO estimates roughly a third of food produced is lost or wasted.

koreanWave.title: K-food wave
koreanWave.line: Kimchi, ramyeon and tteokbokki travelled with Korean drama and music; in 2021 the Oxford English Dictionary added kimbap and bulgogi.

regenerative.title: Regenerative sourcing
regenerative.line: Grains from no-till, cover-cropped farms that rebuild soil carbon; large food companies adopted regenerative sourcing targets in the 2020s.

functionalDrinks.title: Functional drinks
functionalDrinks.line: Kombucha, prebiotic sodas and adaptogen drinks take the shelf once held by soda; prebiotic soda brands reached US supermarkets in the early 2020s.

fireCooking.title: Open-fire cooking
fireCooking.line: Wood and charcoal replace gas in destination kitchens, from Patagonian asado to wood-fired ovens; Francis Mallmann is the movement's public face.

thirdWaveCoffee.title: Third-wave coffee
thirdWaveCoffee.line: Origin, varietal and processing are printed like a wine label and roasted light; the term was coined by roaster Trish Rothgeb in 2002.

nightMarkets.title: Night-market street food
nightMarkets.line: Stalls that open after sunset, from Taipei's Shilin to Bangkok and Marrakesh; Jemaa el-Fnaa square joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2008.

kimchi.name: Kimchi
kimchi.origin: Salted napa cabbage fermented with chili and fish sauce; chili reached Korea after the late 16th century, and kimjang was listed by UNESCO in 2013.

samgyetang.name: Samgyetang
samgyetang.origin: A young chicken simmered with glutinous rice, ginseng and jujube; eaten on the bok-nal dog days, a custom that took its present form in the 1900s.

okonomiyaki.name: Okonomiyaki
okonomiyaki.origin: A cabbage and batter griddle cake from Osaka and Hiroshima; it grew out of the cheap flour dishes of postwar food shortages.

tempura.name: Tempura
tempura.origin: Seafood and vegetables in a thin batter, fried; the technique traces to Portuguese missionaries who reached Nagasaki in the 16th century.

pekingDuck.name: Peking duck
pekingDuck.origin: Roast duck with lacquered skin wrapped in thin pancakes; refined in Ming imperial kitchens, and the Beijing house Quanjude opened in 1864.

xiaolongbao.name: Xiaolongbao
xiaolongbao.origin: Steamed soup dumplings whose filling holds gelatinised broth; they are traced to Nanxiang, near Shanghai, in the 19th century.

hamburger.name: Hamburger
hamburger.origin: A ground-beef patty in a bun; the 19th-century 'Hamburg steak' of German immigrants became a sandwich in the United States.

gumbo.name: Gumbo
gumbo.origin: A thick Louisiana stew of roux, okra and seafood or sausage; born in 18th-century New Orleans where West African, French and Choctaw cooking met.

mulgikapsad.name: Mulgikapsad
mulgikapsad.origin: Sauerkraut braised with pork and barley, from the Mulgi region of southern Estonia; a winter farmhouse staple.

kama.name: Kama
kama.origin: A flour of roasted barley, rye, oats and peas, stirred into kefir or milk; an old Estonian peasant food that needed no cooking.

paella.name: Paella
paella.origin: Rice cooked in a wide pan with rabbit, chicken and beans by farm workers in Valencia's rice fields; the name appears in print in the mid-19th century.

gazpacho.name: Gazpacho
gazpacho.origin: A cold Andalusian soup of tomato, cucumber, pepper, bread and olive oil; it took its modern form after the tomato arrived from the Americas.

fishAmok.name: Fish amok
fishAmok.origin: Fish steamed in banana leaf with kroeung spice paste and coconut milk; a Cambodian dish regarded as part of the Khmer royal culinary tradition.

numBanhChok.name: Num banh chok
numBanhChok.origin: Fermented rice noodles under a fish-based green curry broth; known as 'Khmer noodles', sold from morning stalls across Cambodia.

coqAuVin.name: Coq au vin
coqAuVin.origin: Rooster braised in wine with lardons and mushrooms; recorded in cookbooks in the early 20th century and associated with Burgundy.

ratatouille.name: Ratatouille
ratatouille.origin: A Niçoise stew of aubergine, courgette, tomato and pepper in olive oil; the word first meant a rough stew in 18th-century French.

sauerbraten.name: Sauerbraten
sauerbraten.origin: Beef marinated for days in vinegar and spices, then braised; in the Rhineland the sauce is sweetened with raisins and served with dumplings.

spaetzle.name: Spätzle
spaetzle.origin: Egg noodles scraped from a soft dough into boiling water, from Swabia; protected as an EU geographical indication since 2012.

bacalhauABras.name: Bacalhau à Brás
bacalhauABras.origin: Shredded salt cod scrambled with matchstick potatoes, onion and egg; a Lisbon dish said to be named after a cook from the Bairro Alto quarter.

pastelDeNata.name: Pastel de nata
pastelDeNata.origin: An egg-custard tart from the recipe of the Jerónimos monastery monks in Belém, Lisbon; sold at the Belém bakery since 1837.

bunCha.name: Bún chả
bunCha.origin: Charcoal-grilled pork patties served in a sweet-sour fish-sauce broth with rice vermicelli; a lunchtime dish of Hanoi's Old Quarter.

banhXeo.name: Bánh xèo
banhXeo.origin: A crisp turmeric rice-flour crêpe folded over shrimp and bean sprouts, from southern Vietnam; the name refers to the sizzle of batter in the pan.

rendang.name: Rendang
rendang.origin: Beef reduced for hours in coconut milk and spices; a Minangkabau dish from West Sumatra with roots in ceremonial cooking.

satay.name: Satay
satay.origin: Skewered, marinated meat grilled over charcoal; thought to have developed in 19th-century Java under the influence of Arab and Indian traders' kebabs.

borscht.name: Borscht
borscht.origin: A beet-red vegetable soup that originated in Ukraine and spread across Russian tables; Ukrainian borscht culture was inscribed by UNESCO in 2022.

pelmeni.name: Pelmeni
pelmeni.origin: Small meat dumplings in thin dough, frozen outdoors through Ural and Siberian winters; the name comes from a Uralic word meaning 'ear bread'.

biryani.name: Biryani
biryani.origin: Spiced meat and basmati rice layered and steamed; developed in Mughal court kitchens, with Hyderabad and Lucknow among the famous regional styles.

masalaDosa.name: Masala dosa
masalaDosa.origin: A thin fermented rice-and-lentil crêpe filled with spiced potato; a South Indian dish popularised through the Udupi restaurant tradition of Karnataka.

risottoAllaMilanese.name: Risotto alla milanese
risottoAllaMilanese.origin: Saffron-yellow risotto from Milan; tradition ties it to a 16th-century tale of a glassmaker working on the Duomo.

lasagna.name: Lasagna
lasagna.origin: Wide pasta sheets layered with ragù, béchamel and cheese and baked; a Bolognese tradition whose pasta name descends from the Greco-Roman laganum.

kebap.name: Kebap
kebap.origin: The family of Turkish grilled and roasted meats; the vertical-spit döner is traced to Bursa in the 19th-century Ottoman Empire.

baklava.name: Baklava
baklava.origin: Layers of filo, nuts and syrup; the pastry reached its present form in the kitchens of the Ottoman Topkapı Palace.

greenCurry.name: Green curry
greenCurry.origin: Green chili, galangal and kaffir lime paste in coconut milk; first recorded in Bangkok cookbooks in the early 20th century.

somTam.name: Som tam
somTam.origin: Green papaya pounded in a mortar with chili, lime and fish sauce; it spread to Bangkok from Laos and Thailand's Isan region.

pierogi.name: Pierogi
pierogi.origin: Half-moon dumplings filled with potato and cheese, cabbage or fruit; a medieval arrival in Poland that became the national comfort dish.

bigos.name: Bigos
bigos.origin: 'Hunter's stew' of sauerkraut, fresh cabbage and assorted meats simmered for hours; described in Adam Mickiewicz's 1834 epic Pan Tadeusz.

stamppot.name: Stamppot
stamppot.origin: Potatoes mashed with kale or carrot and onion, served with smoked sausage; a winter dish that settled in once the potato became a Dutch staple.

stroopwafel.name: Stroopwafel
stroopwafel.origin: Two thin waffles pressed around caramel syrup; made in Gouda since the late 18th or early 19th century.

adobo.name: Adobo
adobo.origin: Meat braised in vinegar, soy sauce and garlic; the Spanish name dates from the 16th-century colonial era, but the vinegar-braising method is older.

sinigang.name: Sinigang
sinigang.origin: A soup soured with tamarind, cooked with pork or shrimp and vegetables; a Filipino home dish suited to the tropical climate.

fishAndChips.name: Fish and chips
fishAndChips.origin: Battered white fish with fried potatoes; Jewish immigrants' fried fish met the chip, and the first shops opened in London and Lancashire in the 1860s.

sundayRoast.name: Sunday roast
sundayRoast.origin: Roast meat with potatoes, vegetables, Yorkshire pudding and gravy; the Yorkshire pudding recipe first appeared in print in 1737.

moleNegro.name: Mole negro
moleNegro.origin: Oaxaca's black sauce of many chilies, chocolate and spices; indigenous chili sauces merged with European ingredients after the Spanish conquest.

pozole.name: Pozole
pozole.origin: A soup of nixtamalised hominy corn and meat; a ritual dish of the Aztec era, recorded in 16th-century Spanish chronicles.

feijoada.name: Feijoada
feijoada.origin: Black beans stewed with assorted cuts of pork; rooted in Portuguese bean stews, and now the Wednesday and Saturday lunch across Brazil.

moqueca.name: Moqueca
moqueca.origin: Fish stewed in a clay pot with coconut milk, dendê palm oil, tomato and coriander; a Bahian dish where indigenous cooking met African palm oil.

asado.name: Asado
asado.origin: Beef grilled slowly over embers; Argentina's barbecue culture began with the open-air cooking of 19th-century Pampas gauchos.

empanadas.name: Empanadas
empanadas.origin: Half-moon pastries filled with meat, onion, egg and olives; brought from Galicia, with fillings that differ from Salta to Tucumán.

moussaka.name: Moussaka
moussaka.origin: Layered aubergine and minced meat under béchamel; chef Nikolaos Tselementes added the French sauce in the 1920s to create the modern version.

souvlaki.name: Souvlaki
souvlaki.origin: Small pieces of meat grilled on a skewer; stone skewer supports were unearthed at the Minoan site of Akrotiri on Santorini.

koshari.name: Koshari
koshari.origin: Rice, macaroni and lentils under tomato sauce and fried onions; an Egyptian street dish influenced by Indian khichdi during 19th-century British rule.

fulMedames.name: Ful medames
fulMedames.origin: Fava beans cooked slowly overnight and dressed with olive oil, lemon and cumin; an old Egyptian breakfast whose name is thought to come from Coptic.

tagine.name: Tagine
tagine.origin: Meat and vegetables cooked slowly under a conical clay lid; the word names the pot itself, and the dish appears in medieval Arabic cookbooks.

couscous.name: Couscous
couscous.origin: Steamed semolina granules served with stew, a Berber dish of North Africa; inscribed by UNESCO in 2020 for Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Mauritania.

injera.name: Injera
injera.origin: A sour, spongy flatbread from fermented teff batter; built on teff, a grain domesticated in the Ethiopian highlands.

doroWat.name: Doro wat
doroWat.origin: Chicken and hard-boiled eggs in a berbere and onion stew; the dish served when Ethiopian Orthodox fasting ends on feast days.

ceviche.name: Ceviche
ceviche.origin: Raw fish cured in lime juice with chili and onion; limes arrived with the Spanish, and Peruvian ceviche was inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.

lomoSaltado.name: Lomo saltado
lomoSaltado.origin: Beef stir-fried in a wok with onion, tomato and fried potatoes; a chifa dish born from the wok technique of 19th-century Cantonese immigrants to Peru.

meatPie.name: Meat pie
meatPie.origin: A hand-sized pie of minced beef and gravy; it came with 19th-century British settlers and became the food of Australian football grounds.

lamington.name: Lamington
lamington.origin: Sponge cake dipped in chocolate and rolled in coconut; named around 1900 after Lord Lamington, then Governor of Queensland.

rice.solar: Rice fixes carbon through the C3 pathway; glucose made in the leaf is stored in the grain as starch, amylose and amylopectin.
rice.chemistry: Texture follows the amylose-to-amylopectin ratio; less amylose means stickier rice, and the aroma of fresh rice comes from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline.
rice.pairing: White rice carries a high glycaemic load; pairing it with vegetables, protein and water keeps the post-lunch work rhythm steadier.

wheat.solar: Wheat stores C3-photosynthesis sugars in the endosperm as starch and the reserve proteins glutenin and gliadin, which we eat as bread and noodles.
wheat.chemistry: Kneading links glutenin and gliadin into a gluten network; baking drives the Maillard reaction that gives the crust its colour and toasted aroma.
wheat.pairing: Whole wheat has a lower glycaemic load than refined flour, which suits a morning focus block; take it with water so the fibre can do its work.

maize.solar: Maize uses C4 photosynthesis, fixing carbon efficiently under strong sun and heat, and stores the energy as starch in the kernel.
maize.chemistry: The storage protein zein locks up niacin; nixtamalisation in limewater releases that niacin and creates the characteristic tortilla aroma.
maize.pairing: Nixtamalised tortillas eaten with beans complete the essential amino acids, a steady base for work that runs into the evening.

coffee.solar: The coffee shrub stores C3-photosynthesis sugars in its cherries and seeds; the 2 kcal figure is for brewed coffee, since the roasted bean itself holds several hundred kcal per 100 g.
coffee.chemistry: Caffeine gives the bitterness and the lift, chlorogenic acids the acidity and body, and trigonelline breaks down in roasting into the pyridines and pyrazines that carry the aroma.
coffee.pairing: Caffeine's half-life is about five hours, so a cup after 3 pm can still be present at bedtime; keep it to the morning and early afternoon, with water alongside.

cacao.solar: The shade-grown cacao tree makes C3-photosynthesis sugars and stores them in the seed as fat, cocoa butter, and polyphenols; 70 % dark chocolate holds about 598 kcal per 100 g.
cacao.chemistry: Theobromine gives the bitterness and gentle stimulation, phenylethylamine is present in small amounts, flavanols bring astringency, and fermentation and roasting build the chocolate aroma.
cacao.pairing: Theobromine is a milder stimulant than caffeine, so a square or two in the afternoon disturbs sleep less; 70 % or higher keeps the sugar and the glycaemic swing low.

chili.solar: Chili stores C3-photosynthesis sugars in the fruit and synthesises capsaicin in the placental tissue; native to the Americas, it spread across Asia after the 16th century.
chili.chemistry: The heat is capsaicin triggering the TRPV1 receptor, a sensation of pain rather than taste; capsanthin gives the red colour and the fruit's own sugars the sweetness.
chili.pairing: Capsaicin briefly raises sweating and alertness, which can cut through a post-lunch lull; on a sensitive stomach a milder plate suits late-night work better.

tomato.solar: Tomato stores C3-photosynthesis sugars in the fruit and builds the red pigment lycopene as it ripens; at about 18 kcal per 100 g it is more than 90 % water.
tomato.chemistry: Glutamate gives the umami, lycopene the red, and citric and malic acids the tang; cooking raises both the free glutamate and the availability of lycopene.
tomato.pairing: High in water and potassium, it helps hydration through long screen sessions, and its low glycaemic load leaves afternoon focus undisturbed.

cabbageFerment.solar: Napa cabbage stores C3-photosynthesis sugars in its leaves; during fermentation lactic acid bacteria convert that sugar into lactic acid, leaving about 15 kcal per 100 g.
cabbageFerment.chemistry: Lactic acid gives the sourness, allyl isothiocyanate and sulphur compounds from the brassica and garlic the sharp aroma, and glutamate from the fish sauce the umami.
cabbageFerment.pairing: Low in calories and rich in fibre and lactic acid bacteria, it lightens a heavy lunch; the sodium is high, so pair it with plenty of water at night.
